clue.text: The idea that I frequently haven't

definitions.text: The idea that I frequently haven't

parts.words: The idea that I frequently haven't
parts.note: the stock confession 'I haven't the ___ idea' is completed by the superlative of distant, the idea most often lacking

explanation.surface: Someone admits that ideas are often in short supply.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a dig at the speaker's wits; really it points to the set phrase 'I haven't the remotest idea', so the answer is the word that fills that idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of distant fills the idiom 'not the faintest notion', the kind of idea a puzzled speaker claims not to have.

clue.text: Pelt providing many pelts?

explanation.surface: A furrier's dream source: something supplying plenty of animal skins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pelt' as a verb means pour heavily; the second reading takes the idiom literally, a downpour of animals and so a supply of their fur pelts.
explanation.definitionFit: To pelt is to pour down in torrents, the idiom for heavy rain; read literally, the idiom showers furry animals whose skins are pelts.

clue.text: Low poles held in animal

parts.note: to low is to make the noise of cattle, written moo
S and E, south and east, taken loosely as poles or cardinal points of the compass

explanation.surface: Short posts are kept inside an animal enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like an adjective for the poles; it is the verb for a cow's call. Compass points are usually N and S as poles, so E standing as a pole is loose, as old clues often were.
explanation.definitionFit: An elk of North America is an example of a large deer, a wild animal.

clue.text: Cross the lines after the car-spraying

annotationWithheld.why: Cross the lines after the car-spraying (8): VERSE is 'lines' and 'Cross' defines, but nothing in 'the car-spraying' as held gives TRA; a search of the exact text finds no other wording or parse
annotationWithheld.clue: Cross the lines after the car-spraying

clue.text: Playground music?

explanation.surface: Tunes heard where children play.
explanation.definitionFit: A seat hung on chains is a fixture of any children's play area; it is also big-band jazz of the 1930s and 1940s.

clue.text: Poor shelter from the sea air.

explanation.surface: A shabby hut offering little protection from the salty breeze off the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sea air' looks like breeze, but 'air' means tune: a sailors' work song. The other sense is a crude hut.
explanation.definitionFit: A ramshackle hut is a poor dwelling; a sailors' work song is a tune or air of the sea.

clue.text: Present with past not far off

parts.note: present means here, in attendance
past means by, as in 'walk past' or 'walk by'

explanation.surface: Today and yesterday are close neighbours in time.
explanation.walkthrough: Today's sense is 'by this means', but the word once also meant close at hand, which is the sense defined here.
explanation.definitionFit: In old usage the word meant close by or near at hand, so it means nearby.

clue.text: A granule I dispensed for pain

indicators.note: dispensed suggests a pharmacist making up a remedy, so the letters of these words are made up anew

explanation.surface: A pharmacist hands out a pill as a cure for an ache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dispensed' rearranges the letters of A GRANULE I.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerve pain, often sharp and shooting along a nerve, is one kind of pain.

clue.text: When pressed for. cash give

parts.note: describes someone soft enough to hand over money when asked for a loan, a touch being slang for a request for cash, and also anything soft that gives when pushed

explanation.surface: Someone short of money and asked for a loan hands it over anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'touch' is slang for asking someone for money; the phrase usually describes something soft that gives under the fingers. The stray full stop is a misprint in the newspaper text.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft things give under pressure from fingers, and a soft touch hands over money when asked, so both senses mean giving way when pressed.

clue.text: Dine out, carrying very little money? It's not the proper thing to, do

definitions.text: not the proper thing to, do

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece carries the second on its back, so it sits on top
out suggests something put out of place, so the letters of dine are jumbled

parts.note: a cent is a coin worth very little

explanation.surface: Eating out with almost no money in your pocket is bad form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' jumbles the dining word; 'carrying' works because in a down clue the first piece bears the coin on its back. The comma after 'to' is a newspaper misprint.
explanation.definitionFit: Indecent behaviour offends against decorum, so it is improper conduct.

clue.text: A lotion is the alternative to quarantine

indicators.note: an alternative form of these words is a different arrangement of their letters

explanation.surface: Instead of being shut away, a patient could use some cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alternative' rearranges the letters of A LOTION IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Quarantine is the enforced separation of the sick or exposed from others, a keeping apart.

clue.text: Come to the river — an English one

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for river
the Ouse is a river in England, one of several of that name

explanation.surface: An invitation to meet beside an English waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come to' looks like 'go to', a direction; it means regain consciousness. The Ouse is a river in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to is to wake or stir from sleep or a faint, the intransitive sense of the answer.

clue.text: Tick on sheep? No, sheep on tick here

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece written on another follows it

parts.note: on tick means on credit, abbreviated CR
a ewe is a female sheep

explanation.surface: A parasite sits on a sheep; no, the animal sits on the bug.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'Tick on sheep? No,' is a tease; the second order gives the wordplay. Crewe is a railway town in Cheshire, England, indicated by 'here'.
explanation.definitionFit: A clue answer that is a place may be defined as 'here'; Crewe is a town, a location where one might be.

clue.text: A large stoneware jug holding sage

explanation.surface: A big earthenware pitcher containing a culinary herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sage' looks like the herb, which would fit the jug; it means a wise old man.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellied stoneware jug with a bearded face was called this; an old man with a grey beard is a sage elder.

clue.text: Kind of dog encountered at the printers?

parts.note: kind means type or sort
a setter is a breed of gun dog

explanation.surface: A breed of hound met in a print shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes a person who arranges letters for printing, someone met in a print shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Compositors who set letters ready for the press work in print shops, so they are met there.

clue.text: Poverty-stricken? Prune bad debts

indicators.note: bad means spoiled, so the letters of prune go wrong

parts.note: IOUs are written promises to pay, so debts

explanation.surface: A destitute person should cut down what they owe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prune' looks like a verb telling you to cut debts; it is anagram fodder, made 'bad', and the debts are written promises to pay.
explanation.definitionFit: A penurious person is extremely poor, lacking money.

clue.text: The first modern job centre? It's.14th century!

indicators.note: the first of the word The is its opening letter

parts.note: modern means recent

indicators.note: the centre of the word job is its middle letter

explanation.surface: An exclamation that the very first employment exchange dates back to the 1300s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'job centre' looks like a single thing, a UK state employment office; 'centre' instead takes the middle letter O of 'job'. The Italian name for the 1300s counts them as the three hundreds.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian term for the 1300s names that period of art and literature, the fourteenth century.

clue.text: A private American ring for money-changing

parts.note: a GI is an American private soldier
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: An American soldier wears a ring while changing money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'private' looks like an adjective for the ring; it is a rank, the US soldier GI.
explanation.definitionFit: The fee charged for exchanging one currency for another is a charge on money-changing.

clue.text: Having lost status, banker entertains group of students

indicators.note: to entertain is to take in as a guest, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: a banker is something with banks, a river; the Dee is a river
a class is a group of students

explanation.surface: A disgraced financier hosts some students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banker' looks like a financier; in crosswords it is a river, here the Dee in Scotland and Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who has come down in the social world has lost rank or standing.

clue.text: Outbreak can upset the English

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of can are disturbed

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A disturbance in a tin unsettles the English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outbreak' suggests disease or war; here it is spots breaking out on the skin, and 'upset' scrambles the tin.
explanation.definitionFit: An eruption of spots on the skin is a rash or breakout of pimples.

clue.text: An eruption alters then alters

indicators.note: the repeated word alters means changes, so the letters of the previous two words are changed

explanation.surface: A volcano's eruption changes one thing, then changes another.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'alters' is fodder with 'then'; the second 'alters' rearranges ALTERS THEN. 'eruption' means a skin rash, not a volcano.
explanation.definitionFit: An itchy rash of weals from stinging plants is a skin eruption.

clue.text: Make a hasty exit when the English go in and yell

indicators.note: go in means enter, so one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: to scram is to leave in a hurry
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone flees and shrieks when the English arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go in' puts E inside SCRAM.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud cry of fear or pain is a yell or shriek.

clue.text: Costing the earth? Quite the contrary

definitions.text: Costing the earth? Quite the contrary

parts.words: Costing the earth? Quite the contrary
parts.note: costing a fortune is the usual sense; taken literally, costing only soil, the thing is very inexpensive

explanation.surface: Something is not expensive at all, despite appearances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Costing the earth' normally means costing a fortune; 'quite the contrary' flips that, and 'earth' read as soil gives the idiom for very inexpensive.
explanation.definitionFit: Something priced as low as soil is very inexpensive, a bargain.

clue.text: Flat obtained by Public Relations unit

parts.note: one is the unit number

explanation.surface: An apartment bought by a publicity department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like an apartment; it means lying face down.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying stretched out face down is lying horizontal, so the answer means level or prostrate.

clue.text: Allowed some publicity

indicators.note: some of the word publicity means a part of its letters

explanation.surface: A certain amount of press coverage is permitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' picks LICIT out of 'publicity'.
explanation.definitionFit: Licit means lawful or permitted.

clue.text: Net — to prevent folk having this view through your window?

definitions.text: to prevent folk having this view through your window?

explanation.surface: Lace curtains stop passers-by looking in through the glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Net' looks like a curtain fabric; it means left after deductions, as in net profit. The second reading is a cryptic hint: net curtains stop people having an unobstructed view.
explanation.definitionFit: Clear profit is the amount after deductions, net; and an unobstructed view through glass is the view net curtains block.

clue.text: Wizard country, unique for the invigorating air

parts.note: Oz is the land in The Wizard of Oz
one means unique, single of its kind

explanation.surface: A fantasy land, one of a kind, known for its bracing atmosphere.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition uses the popular sense of fresh seaside air, not the chemistry.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh bracing sea air was popularly called this gas, an invigorating breeze.

clue.text: Model gets painter to provide special clothing

parts.note: the Model T was the Ford car, so T
Henri Rousseau was a French painter

explanation.surface: A fashion model gets an artist to supply a costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like a fashion model; it is the Ford Model T, giving T.
explanation.definitionFit: A bride's collection of clothes and linen for married life is a special set of clothing.

clue.text: Look around Uncle's oil plant

indicators.note: around means one piece goes round the other

parts.note: look means see
Uncle Sam stands for the USA, so Uncle gives Sam

explanation.surface: Inspect your uncle's vegetable oil crop.
explanation.walkthrough: Uncle Sam personifies the United States; 'around' wraps the looking word round him.
explanation.definitionFit: The seeds of this plant are pressed for cooking oil, so it is an oil-bearing crop.

clue.text: Arch-seer put out by investigation

indicators.note: put out means disturbed, so the letters of arch-seer are rearranged

explanation.surface: A chief prophet is upset by an inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out' looks like 'annoyed'; it rearranges the letters of ARCH-SEER.
explanation.definitionFit: Research is systematic study, an inquiry into a subject.
